answer_text:
Let \(a,b,c\) be the sides opposite \(\angle A,\angle B,\angle C\), respectively.

By the Law of Sines,

\[
a:b:c=\sin A:\sin B:\sin C.
\]

The condition

\[
bc=b^2-a^2
\]

becomes, after canceling the common sine-law constant,

\[
\sin B\sin C=\sin^2 B-\sin^2 A.
\]

Use the identity

\[
\sin^2 B-\sin^2 A=\sin(A+B)\sin(B-A).
\]

Since \(A+B=180^\circ-C\), we have \(\sin(A+B)=\sin C\). Therefore,

\[
\sin B\sin C=\sin C\sin(B-A).
\]

Because \(C\) is an angle of a nondegenerate triangle, \(\sin C\neq 0\), so we can divide by \(\sin C\):

\[
\sin B=\sin(B-A).
\]

Given \(B-A=80^\circ\),

\[
\sin B=\sin 80^\circ.
\]

Since \(A>0\), we have \(B>80^\circ\). Also \(A+B<180^\circ\), so \(B<130^\circ\). In this range, the only solution to \(\sin B=\sin 80^\circ\) is

\[
B=100^\circ.
\]

Thus

\[
A=B-80^\circ=20^\circ,
\]

and

\[
C=180^\circ-A-B=180^\circ-20^\circ-100^\circ=60^\circ.
\]

\[
\boxed{60}
\]
